In Joyce’s _Ulysses_, Leopold Bloom recalls that Molly called the Greek word for it “met him pike hoses”

trap.title: Not karma, not resurrection
trap.body: Reincarnation tossups are full of neighboring ideas. Karma is the force of a person’s actions that shapes the next life, samsara is the whole cycle of birth and death, and moksha or nirvana is the escape from it. Resurrection, the raising of the dead taught in Christianity, Islam, and Judaism, is a different idea, and so is incarnation, a god taking bodily form, as with Vishnu’s avatars.
trap.fix: If the question describes a soul or self returning in a new body, say reincarnation; rebirth, transmigration of souls, and metempsychosis are accepted. “This force of actions” means karma, “this cycle” means samsara, and “this liberation” means moksha or nirvana.
trap.line: Real answer line: reincarnation (accept rebirth, transmigration of souls, or metempsychosis; do not accept “samsara,” “karma,” “resurrection,” or “nirvana”)

topics.name: Paul the Apostle
topics.kicker: Apostle to the Gentiles · Missionary and author of New Testament letters
topics.briefing: According to the Acts of the Apostles, a Pharisee named Saul was hunting down followers of Jesus when a blinding light stopped him on the road to Damascus. Known by his Roman name, Paul, he became one of early Christianity’s most important missionaries, traveling around the Mediterranean by land and sea and surviving a shipwreck on Malta. Thirteen of the New Testament’s 27 books are letters traditionally credited to him, and tradition says he was executed in Rome under the emperor Nero.
topics.answerHtml: Paul the Apostle (or Saint Paul or Paul of Tarsus; accept Saul of Tarsus; prompt on Saul; do not accept “Peter”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: In a garden in Milan, Augustine of Hippo heard a child’s voice chanting “Take up and read,” opened a book of scripture, and read a passage from this man’s Letter to the Romans that led to his conversion. Martin Luther later found the heart of his teaching on faith in that letter’s line “The just shall live by faith.”
tossups.r: This apostle also wrote letters to the Corinthians and the Galatians. For 10 points, name this missionary who was converted on the road to Damascus.

tossups.p: According to Acts, while his enemies watched the city gates day and night, this man’s followers lowered him in a basket through an opening in the city wall so that he could escape. Earlier in that same city, a disciple named Ananias [“an-uh-NY-us”] placed his hands on him, and something like scales fell from his eyes.
tossups.r: That city was Damascus. For 10 points, name this apostle who had been blinded by a light on the road there.

tossups.p: In one letter, this man says that after his conversion he went away into Arabia, and that he later opposed Cephas [“SEE-fus”], or Peter, “to his face” at Antioch for pulling away from meals with non-Jewish believers. That letter says that among believers there is “neither Jew nor Greek,” neither slave nor free, because all are one in Christ Jesus.
tossups.r: That letter is addressed to the Galatians. For 10 points, name this author of many New Testament letters, called the Apostle to the Gentiles.

tossups.p: In the shortest letter credited to him, this man asks a believer named Philemon [“fy-LEE-mun”] to welcome back Onesimus [“oh-NESS-ih-mus”], an enslaved man who had left Philemon’s household, “no longer as a slave” but as a dear brother. He wrote that letter while he was a prisoner.
tossups.r: He also wrote letters to the churches in Rome and Corinth. For 10 points, name this apostle who was converted on the road to Damascus.

tossups.p: In a speech in Athens, this man said that in God “we live and move and have our being.” Epicurean and Stoic philosophers had brought him to the Areopagus [“air-ee-OP-uh-gus”], where he spoke about an altar inscribed “To an unknown god.”
tossups.r: His missionary journeys fill much of the second half of the Acts of the Apostles. For 10 points, name this apostle who wrote the Letter to the Romans.

tossups.p: After more than forty men vowed not to eat or drink until they had killed this prisoner, his sister’s son warned a Roman commander, who sent him under heavy guard to the governor Felix in Caesarea [“sess-uh-REE-uh”]. That commander had earlier been alarmed to learn that he had put a Roman citizen in chains.
tossups.r: Later, on trial before the governor Festus, this man declared, “I appeal to Caesar!” For 10 points, name this apostle who was sent to Rome as a prisoner.

tossups.p: Acts says a young man named Eutychus [“YOO-tih-kus”] fell asleep during this man’s long talk and dropped from a third-story window, and that this man brought him back to life. Later, when a viper fastened onto his hand as he put brushwood on a fire, he shook it off without harm, and the islanders decided he must be a god.
tossups.r: He had been shipwrecked on that island, Malta, while being taken to Rome. For 10 points, name this apostle who wrote the Letter to the Romans.

tossups.p: This man called himself “a Hebrew of Hebrews” from the tribe of Benjamin and, as to the law, a Pharisee. According to Acts, he studied in Jerusalem under the respected teacher Gamaliel [“guh-MAY-lee-ul”], and he earned his living as a tentmaker.
tossups.r: He was born in Tarsus, in what is now Turkey. For 10 points, name this apostle who was blinded by a light on the road to Damascus.

tossups.p: In Ephesus [“EF-uh-sus”], handkerchiefs and aprons that had touched this man were carried to the sick, and many people who had practiced magic burned their scrolls. A silversmith named Demetrius started a riot in that city because this man’s preaching was hurting the trade in silver shrines of the goddess Artemis.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this missionary who traveled with Barnabas and Silas and wrote many letters in the New Testament.

tossups.p: The King James Bible’s version of one of this man’s letters says that “now we see through a glass, darkly,” and it ends that chapter by naming faith, hope, and charity, adding that “the greatest of these is charity.” Modern translations of that chapter, often read at weddings, say “Love is patient, love is kind.”
tossups.r: That chapter is in his First Letter to the Corinthians. For 10 points, name this apostle who was converted on the road to Damascus.

tossups.p: Caravaggio [“kar-uh-VAH-jee-oh”] painted this man lying on his back beneath a large horse, with his arms flung open, for a chapel in Rome’s church of Santa Maria del Popolo. In art, this man often holds a sword, a reminder of the tradition that he was executed in Rome under the emperor Nero.
tossups.r: That painting shows the moment he was struck blind on the road to Damascus. For 10 points, name this apostle.

tossups.p: After a sharp disagreement over bringing along John Mark, who had left them partway through an earlier journey, this man and Barnabas went separate ways. This man chose Silas as his new partner, and in a vision a man of Macedonia begged him, “Come over to Macedonia and help us.”
tossups.r: Soon after, a seller of purple cloth named Lydia was baptized in Philippi. For 10 points, name this missionary who later wrote a letter to the church at Philippi.

tossups.p: A letter to Timothy credited to this man says, “I have fought the good fight, I have finished the race, I have kept the faith.” In another letter, he says he was given a “thorn in the flesh” to keep him from becoming conceited, and he lists hardships that include being shipwrecked three times.
tossups.r: Thirteen New Testament letters are traditionally credited to him, though scholars debate whether he wrote all of them. For 10 points, name this Apostle to the Gentiles.

tossups.p: Acts first calls this man by his Roman name in a scene on the island of Cyprus, where he makes a sorcerer named Elymas [“EL-ih-mus”] blind for a time. Later on that journey, a crowd at Lystra [“LISS-truh”] hailed his partner as Zeus and called this man Hermes because he did most of the talking.
tossups.r: That partner was Barnabas. For 10 points, name this apostle, who was also called by the Hebrew name Saul.

tossups.p: Witnesses at the stoning of Stephen laid their cloaks at this young man’s feet, and he approved of that killing. Afterward, according to Acts, he went from house to house dragging believers off to prison, and he asked the high priest for letters allowing him to arrest followers of Jesus in Damascus.
tossups.r: On his way there, a light from heaven blinded him. For 10 points, name this man who became the Apostle to the Gentiles.

clues.t: Acts says he was converted on the road to Damascus when a light from heaven blinded him and a voice said, “I am Jesus, whom you are persecuting”
Called the “Apostle to the Gentiles” for spreading the faith among non-Jews
Wrote many New Testament letters, or epistles, such as Romans, 1 and 2 Corinthians, and Galatians
Born in Tarsus, in modern Turkey; he was also called by his Hebrew name, Saul
Made missionary journeys around the eastern Mediterranean, told in the Acts of the Apostles
Witnesses at Stephen’s stoning laid their cloaks at his feet; afterward he dragged believers off to prison
In Damascus, Acts says, a disciple named Ananias laid hands on him, and something like scales fell from his eyes
First missionary journey with Barnabas; at Lystra, a crowd called Barnabas Zeus and him Hermes
Later traveled with Silas and Timothy; two New Testament letters are addressed to Timothy
In Athens, spoke at the Areopagus (Mars Hill) about an altar inscribed “To an unknown god”
A Pharisee from the tribe of Benjamin who studied under Gamaliel and earned his living as a tentmaker
A Roman citizen by birth, he told the governor Festus, “I appeal to Caesar!” and was sent to Rome
Shipwrecked on Malta on the way to Rome; a viper bit his hand, and he shook it off unharmed
1 Corinthians 13: “Love is patient, love is kind … the greatest of these is love”
Thirteen letters are traditionally credited to him; most scholars agree he wrote at least seven and debate the rest
Tradition says he was executed in Rome under the emperor Nero; in art he often holds a sword
His Letter to the Romans led to Augustine’s conversion (“Take up and read”), and its line “The just shall live by faith” inspired Martin Luther
Escaped Damascus when his followers lowered him in a basket through an opening in the city wall
Galatians: he went into Arabia after his conversion, opposed Cephas (Peter) “to his face” at Antioch, and wrote “neither Jew nor Greek”
His shortest letter asks Philemon to welcome back Onesimus “no longer as a slave” but as a brother
In his Athens speech, he said that in God “we live and move and have our being”; Epicurean and Stoic philosophers had debated him
More than forty men vowed to kill him; his sister’s son warned a Roman commander, who sent him to the governor Felix in Caesarea
Acts says Eutychus fell asleep during his long talk and dropped from a third-story window, and that he brought the young man back to life
In Ephesus, handkerchiefs that touched him were carried to the sick; Demetrius the silversmith led a riot over shrines of Artemis
Caravaggio painted his conversion, showing him on his back beneath a horse, for Santa Maria del Popolo in Rome
Split with Barnabas over John Mark, chose Silas, and saw a vision of a man of Macedonia; Lydia, a seller of purple cloth, was baptized at Philippi
Wrote of a “thorn in the flesh” and of being shipwrecked three times; a letter to Timothy says, “I have fought the good fight”
Acts first uses his Roman name on Cyprus, where he makes the sorcerer Elymas blind for a time

trap.title: Paul or Peter?
trap.body: Paul and Peter are the two great apostles of the Acts of the Apostles, they share a feast day on June 29, and painters often show them side by side, so early buzzers mix them up. Peter was one of Jesus’s twelve disciples; Paul joined the movement after Jesus’s death and was converted on the road to Damascus. A question that asks for the book telling both of their stories wants “Acts,” not either man.
trap.fix: Keys, walking on water, denying Jesus three times, or the first pope in Catholic tradition mean Peter. Tarsus, Damascus, Barnabas, Silas, Malta, the Areopagus, or letters to the Romans, Corinthians, and Galatians mean Paul. Saying only “Saul” earns a prompt, so add “of Tarsus” or just say Paul.
trap.line: Real answer line: Paul the Apostle (or Saint Paul or Paul of Tarsus; accept Saul of Tarsus; prompt on Saul; do not accept “Peter”)

topics.name: Samson
topics.kicker: Strongman of the Book of Judges · His strength lay in his uncut hair
topics.dates: Set in the era of the judges, c. 1200–1000 BCE
topics.briefing: In the Book of Judges, Samson is an Israelite strongman whose power is tied to his hair: before he was born, an angel declared that no razor must ever touch his head. He tears apart a lion with his bare hands, strikes down a thousand Philistines with a donkey’s jawbone, and carries off a city’s gates, until Delilah learns his secret and has his hair cut. Blinded and imprisoned, he prays for strength one last time and pulls down the temple of Dagon.

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: In the Bible, an angel told this man’s mother, the wife of Manoah [“muh-NOH-uh”], that she must not drink wine and that no razor could ever touch her son’s head. When Manoah later offered a sacrifice, the angel rose toward heaven in the flame from the altar.
tossups.r: Her son, a Nazirite from birth, grew up to fight the Philistines. For 10 points, name this biblical strongman whose strength was tied to his uncut hair.

tossups.p: At his wedding feast, this man challenged thirty guests with the riddle “Out of the eater, something to eat; out of the strong, something sweet.” After they pressured his bride into telling them the answer, he complained, “If you had not plowed with my heifer, you would not have solved my riddle.”
tossups.r: The answer was honey that he had found in the body of a lion. For 10 points, name this strongman from the Book of Judges.

tossups.p: The classic tin of Lyle’s Golden Syrup shows bees swarming around a lion’s body and the words “Out of the strong came forth sweetness,” a line from this man’s story. In that story, he found bees and honey inside a lion that he had earlier torn apart with his bare hands.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Nazirite from the Book of Judges whose hair was cut off while he slept on Delilah’s lap.

tossups.p: After his father-in-law gave his wife to another man, this man caught three hundred foxes, tied them tail to tail in pairs with a torch between each pair of tails, and set them loose in the Philistines’ fields, burning their grain, vineyards, and olive groves.
tossups.r: Earlier, he had torn apart a lion with his bare hands. For 10 points, name this biblical strongman who was later betrayed by Delilah.

tossups.p: In the Bible, after a battle at a place called Ramath Lehi [“RAY-muth LEE-hy”], or “Jawbone Hill,” this man was so thirsty that he called out to God, and water poured out of a hollow place in the ground.
tossups.r: In that battle, he had struck down a thousand Philistines with the jawbone of a donkey. For 10 points, name this strongman whose strength came from his uncut hair.

tossups.p: When the people of Gaza waited at the city gate to ambush this man at dawn, he got up at midnight, tore the doors of the gate loose along with the two posts, and carried them on his shoulders to the top of a hill facing Hebron.
tossups.r: Later, the Philistines held him prisoner in that same city after Delilah betrayed him. For 10 points, name this strongman from the Book of Judges.

tossups.p: The rulers of the Philistines each promised a woman from the Valley of Sorek [“SOR-ek”] eleven hundred pieces of silver to learn the secret of this man’s strength. He fooled her three times, claiming he could be held by seven fresh bowstrings, then by new ropes, and then by weaving his seven braids into a loom.
tossups.r: Finally he told that woman, Delilah, the truth about his uncut hair. For 10 points, name this biblical strongman.

tossups.p: About three thousand people were watching from the roof of a temple when this blinded prisoner was brought out to entertain the crowd, and he asked the servant leading him by the hand to let him feel the pillars that held up the building.
tossups.r: That temple belonged to the god Dagon. Praying for strength one last time, he pushed against its two central pillars and brought the temple down on himself and the Philistines. For 10 points, name this biblical strongman.

tossups.p: In a dramatic poem by John Milton, this man laments that he is “Eyeless in Gaza at the mill with slaves,” a phrase that Aldous Huxley later used as the title of a novel. In that poem, a boastful giant named Harapha [“HAR-uh-fuh”] taunts this man, and his father, Manoa, tries to buy his freedom.
tossups.r: In the Bible, he loses his strength when Delilah has his hair cut. For 10 points, name this hero of the Book of Judges.

tossups.p: In an opera by Camille Saint-Saëns [“san-SAHNS”], a woman sings the aria “My heart opens to your voice” to win over this man, and the last act features a wild dance called the Bacchanale [“bah-kuh-NAHL”]. Franz Liszt helped arrange that opera’s 1877 premiere in Weimar [“VY-mar”].
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this biblical strongman who loses his strength when the opera’s title woman, Dalila, has his hair cut.

tossups.p: Peter Paul Rubens painted this man asleep in a woman’s lap while a man carefully cuts his hair by candlelight and soldiers wait at the door. That painting hangs in London’s National Gallery.
tossups.r: In the Bible, this Nazirite lost his great strength once his hair was cut. For 10 points, name this man who was betrayed by Delilah.

tossups.p: George Frideric Handel based an oratorio about this man on a poem by John Milton, and it includes the soprano aria “Let the bright Seraphim.” In the New Testament, the Letter to the Hebrews names this man among heroes of faith, along with Gideon, Barak, and Jephthah [“JEF-thuh”].
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Nazirite whose strength left him after Delilah had his hair cut.

tossups.p: This man’s parents asked why he wanted to marry a Philistine woman from Timnah [“TIM-nuh”] instead of a woman from his own people. On the way to Timnah, a young lion came roaring toward him, and he tore it apart with his bare hands.
tossups.r: He later posed a riddle about that lion at his wedding feast. For 10 points, name this biblical judge whose uncut hair gave him great strength.

tossups.p: This man was buried between Zorah [“ZOR-uh”] and Eshtaol [“ESH-tay-ol”] in the tomb of his father, Manoah, after leading Israel for twenty years. The Book of Judges says that he killed more Philistines when he died than he had while he lived.
tossups.r: He had been dedicated to God as a Nazirite, so no razor was ever supposed to touch his head. For 10 points, name this strongman.

tossups.p: After attacking the Philistines, this man went to live in a cave in the rock of Etam [“EE-tum”], where three thousand men of Judah came to tie him up and hand him over to the Philistines. He let them bind him with two new ropes, but when the Philistines rushed at him, the ropes fell from his arms like burned flax.
tossups.r: He then struck down a thousand Philistines with the jawbone of a donkey. For 10 points, name this biblical strongman.

clues.t: His great strength was tied to his uncut hair
Delilah learned his secret and had his hair cut off while he slept, so his strength left him
A strongman and leader of Israel in the Book of Judges, in the Hebrew Bible (Old Testament)
Fought the Philistines, enemies of the Israelites
Blinded and captured, he pushed against the pillars of the temple of Dagon, bringing it down on himself and the Philistines
Dedicated to God as a Nazirite from birth, so no razor could touch his head
Tore apart a young lion with his bare hands on the way to Timnah
Wedding riddle: “Out of the eater, something to eat; out of the strong, something sweet” (honey in the lion)
Struck down a thousand Philistines with the jawbone of a donkey
Tied torches between the tails of 300 foxes, in pairs, and sent them into the Philistines’ fields
Carried off the doors and posts of Gaza’s city gate to a hill facing Hebron
The Philistines blinded him and made him grind grain in a prison in Gaza
Son of Manoah, of the tribe of Dan; an angel announced his birth to his mother
Camille Saint-Saëns’s 1877 opera about him: Dalila sings “My heart opens to your voice,” and Liszt helped arrange its premiere in Weimar
In John Milton’s dramatic poem about him, he is “Eyeless in Gaza at the mill with slaves,” and the giant Harapha taunts him
The classic Lyle’s Golden Syrup tin shows bees around a lion with the words “Out of the strong came forth sweetness”
Told his wedding guests, “If you had not plowed with my heifer, you would not have solved my riddle”
Each Philistine ruler offered Delilah, of the Valley of Sorek, 1,100 pieces of silver for his secret
His false answers to Delilah: seven fresh bowstrings, new ropes, and weaving his seven braids into a loom
At Ramath Lehi (“Jawbone Hill”), Judges says God made water pour from a hollow in the ground when he was thirsty
Lived in a cave in the rock of Etam; 3,000 men of Judah tied him with new ropes, which fell off like burned flax
About 3,000 people watched from the temple roof; he asked the servant leading him to let him feel the pillars
Led Israel 20 years and was buried between Zorah and Eshtaol in his father Manoah’s tomb
Hebrews 11 lists him among heroes of faith with Gideon, Barak, and Jephthah; Handel wrote an oratorio about him
Rubens painted him asleep in Delilah’s lap as a man cuts his hair (National Gallery, London)
In Judges, when Manoah offered a sacrifice, the angel who announced the birth rose toward heaven in the altar’s flame

trap.title: The strongman, not Delilah
trap.body: Many Samson clues are really about the people around him, so early buzzers grab the wrong name. Delilah is the woman who betrayed him, and Manoah is his father. Gideon and Jephthah are other judges in the same book, and Samuel, whose name starts the same way, is the later judge who anointed Saul as king. A question can also ask for a work about him, such as Milton’s _Samson Agonistes_ or Saint-Saëns’s opera _Samson et Dalila_.
trap.fix: If the question says “this man” or “this judge” and mentions long hair, a lion, foxes, a jawbone, or pillars, say Samson. Say Delilah only for “this woman.” If it asks for “this poem” or “this opera,” give the title instead.
trap.line: Real answer line: Samson (accept Shimshon; do not accept “Delilah”)

topics.name: Shabbat
topics.kicker: Jewish day of rest · From Friday sundown to Saturday nightfall
topics.dates: Every week, Friday sundown to Saturday nightfall
topics.briefing: Every Friday evening, many Jewish families light candles, bless wine and two braided loaves of challah, and greet one another with “Shabbat shalom.” Shabbat, the weekly day of rest, recalls the story in Genesis in which God rests on the seventh day of creation, and the commandment to “remember the Sabbath day, to keep it holy.” It lasts until Saturday night, when a short ceremony called Havdalah separates it from the new week.
topics.answerHtml: Shabbat (or Sabbath; accept Shabbos or Shabbes; prompt on Saturday or “day of rest”; do not accept “Sunday”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: The essayist Ahad Ha’am [“ah-KHAHD hah-AHM”] wrote that more than the Jewish people have kept this observance, it has kept the Jewish people. The Book of Exodus calls it a sign between God and the Israelites forever, and observant Jews avoid thirty-nine categories of work during it.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this weekly Jewish day of rest, which begins at sundown on Friday.

tossups.p: To end this period, people smell fragrant spices from a decorated box and hold their fingertips up to a braided candle with several wicks, which is then put out in a little wine. Many people wait until three stars can be seen in the sky before starting that ceremony.
tossups.r: That ceremony is called Havdalah, meaning “separation.” For 10 points, name this weekly Jewish day of rest that lasts from Friday evening to Saturday night.

tossups.p: In the 1500s, Shlomo Alkabetz [“ahl-kah-BETS”] of Safed [“SAH-fed”] wrote a hymn that welcomes this day as a bride, with the refrain “Come, my beloved, to greet the bride.” That hymn, “Lekha Dodi” [“leh-KHAH doh-DEE”], is sung in synagogues on Friday evenings.
tossups.r: At home, families mark its start by lighting candles and blessing wine and two loaves of challah. For 10 points, name this weekly day of rest in Judaism.

tossups.p: In the Book of Exodus, a commandment says to “remember” this day because God made the world in six days, while a version in Deuteronomy says to “observe” it and recalls the Israelites’ slavery in Egypt. The two candles lit to welcome it are often said to stand for those two verbs.
tossups.r: In Genesis, God rests on the seventh day of creation. For 10 points, name this weekly Jewish day of rest.

tossups.p: Some neighborhoods are surrounded by an eruv [“AIR-uv”], a boundary often made of wire strung between poles, so that observant people may carry things such as house keys outdoors during this time. Some elevators in Israel stop at every floor automatically during it, so riders don’t have to press buttons.
tossups.r: Families welcome it by lighting candles. For 10 points, name this Jewish day of rest that begins on Friday evening.

tossups.p: Two loaves of bread are set out for this day’s meals to recall the Exodus story of the double portion of manna gathered on the sixth day, since none fell on the seventh. Those braided loaves are covered with a cloth while a blessing over wine called Kiddush [“KID-ish”] is said.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this weekly Jewish day of rest, whose arrival is marked by lighting candles.

tossups.p: Abraham Joshua Heschel [“HESH-ul”] wrote a 1951 book describing this day as “a palace in time.” The prophet Isaiah urged people to call it “a delight,” and many synagogues hold a reception called an oneg [“OH-neg”], meaning “delight,” after Friday night services.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this weekly Jewish day of rest, which many families begin with a festive Friday night dinner.

tossups.p: Because cooking is not allowed during this time, many families prepare a stew of beans, barley, potatoes, and meat called cholent [“CHAW-lunt”] beforehand and keep it warm overnight for the next day’s lunch. Some ovens and refrigerators have a special mode named for this day.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this weekly day of rest that observant Jews keep from Friday sundown to Saturday nightfall.

tossups.p: On Friday nights, many families sing “Shalom Aleichem” [“shah-LOHM ah-LAY-khem”] to welcome the angels who, according to tradition, walk people home from the synagogue on this day. Families may also sing “A Woman of Valor,” a passage from the Book of Proverbs, and bless their children.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Jewish day of rest, whose name people pair with the word “shalom” as a greeting.

tossups.p: A section of the Mishnah named for this observance lists thirty-nine main kinds of forbidden work, including plowing, writing two letters, lighting a fire, and carrying an object from a private area into a public one.
tossups.r: Rabbis linked that list to the work of building the Tabernacle in the wilderness. For 10 points, name this weekly Jewish day of rest.

tossups.p: In the Gospel of Mark, after Pharisees criticize his disciples for picking heads of grain on this day, Jesus says that it “was made for man, not man for” it. Seventh-day Adventists also keep this day of rest on Saturday.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this weekly day of rest that Jews keep from Friday evening to Saturday night.

tossups.p: Many communities light candles eighteen minutes before sunset to begin this period, and the woman of the house traditionally covers her eyes while saying the blessing over them. It ends about twenty-five hours after it begins, once night has fallen on Saturday.
tossups.r: Families then bless wine and two loaves of challah. For 10 points, name this weekly Jewish day of rest that begins on Friday evening.

tossups.p: In the Bible, Nehemiah ordered the gates of Jerusalem shut at dusk before this day began, so that merchants could not come in to sell their goods. Rabbis also limited how far people may walk beyond their town during it to two thousand cubits.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this weekly Jewish day of rest, which begins at sundown on Friday.

tossups.p: Under the principle of pikuach nefesh [“pih-KOO-akh NEH-fesh”], the rules of this day must be set aside to save a life. During the Maccabean revolt, Mattathias [“mat-uh-THY-us”] and his followers decided that they would fight to defend themselves even on this day.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this weekly Jewish day of rest, when observant Jews avoid thirty-nine kinds of work.

tossups.p: On the morning of this day, seven people are called up to the Torah as synagogues read the week’s portion, so that in most synagogues the whole scroll is read in a year. Many boys celebrate their bar mitzvah on this day by reading from the Torah before the congregation.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this weekly Jewish day of rest that begins at sundown on Friday.

It ends about 25 hours after it begins, once three stars can be seen on Saturday night
The Friday evening hymn “Lekha Dodi” welcomes it as a bride
That morning, seven people are called up to read the week’s Torah portion; many bar mitzvahs happen then
Cooking is not allowed, so families keep a slow-cooked stew called cholent warm overnight
Ahad Ha’am: more than the Jewish people have kept it, it has kept the Jewish people
The Book of Exodus calls it a sign between God and the Israelites forever
Exodus says to “remember” it (God made the world in six days); Deuteronomy says to “observe” it (slavery in Egypt); two candles stand for the two verbs
Shlomo Alkabetz of Safed wrote “Lekha Dodi” in the 1500s: “Come, my beloved, to greet the bride”
Some elevators in Israel stop at every floor automatically during it, so riders don’t press buttons
Abraham Joshua Heschel’s 1951 book calls it “a palace in time”
Isaiah calls it “a delight”; an oneg (“delight”) is a reception after Friday night services
The Friday night song “Shalom Aleichem” welcomes angels said to walk people home; families sing “A Woman of Valor” from Proverbs
A Mishnah section named for it lists the 39 kinds of work, such as plowing, writing two letters, and lighting a fire
In Mark’s Gospel, Jesus says it “was made for man”; Seventh-day Adventists keep it on Saturday
Many communities light candles 18 minutes before sunset; the woman of the house traditionally covers her eyes for the blessing

trap.title: Weekly, not yearly
trap.body: This answer is the weekly day of rest, but nearby answer lines are yearly holidays: Rosh Hashanah, the New Year, and Yom Kippur, the Day of Atonement, which Leviticus calls a “Sabbath of Sabbaths.” Its customs, like candles, wine, and challah, show up in holiday questions too. And most Christians hold their main worship on Sunday, which they call the Lord’s Day; “Sunday” is not accepted here.
trap.fix: Listen for “weekly,” “every Friday,” Havdalah, the 39 kinds of work, or the eruv: those mean Shabbat (“Sabbath” and “Shabbos” also work). A shofar, apples and honey, or Kol Nidre mean one of the High Holy Days. “Saturday” alone earns only a prompt, so say “Shabbat” or “Sabbath.”
trap.line: Real answer line: Shabbat (or Sabbath; accept Shabbos or Shabbes; prompt on Saturday or “day of rest”; do not accept “Sunday”)

topics.name: Torah
topics.kicker: Judaism’s holiest text · The five books from Genesis to Deuteronomy
topics.briefing: The Torah is Judaism’s holiest text: the five books from Genesis to Deuteronomy, which Jewish tradition says God gave to Moses at Mount Sinai. In synagogues it is handwritten on a parchment scroll by a trained scribe, and readers follow its words with a pointer called a yad so their fingers never touch the parchment. Each fall, on Simchat Torah, communities dance with the scrolls as they finish the yearly reading and start again from “In the beginning.”
topics.answerHtml: Torah (or Pentateuch or Five Books of Moses; accept Chumash or Tawrat; prompt on Tanakh, Hebrew Bible, or Old Testament; do not accept “Talmud”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: One opinion in the Talmud says that Joshua wrote the last eight verses of this text, which describe how Moses died after seeing the Promised Land from Mount Nebo [“NEE-boh”]. Jewish tradition holds that Moses wrote down the rest of it as God gave it to him.
tossups.r: It begins with the Book of Genesis and ends with Deuteronomy. For 10 points, name this collection of the first five books of the Hebrew Bible.

tossups.p: A scribe called a sofer [“SOH-fer”] copies this text by hand with a quill on parchment, and a single mistake that is not fixed makes a scroll unfit to use. Each finished scroll is wound on two wooden rollers called “trees of life.”
tossups.r: It is kept in the synagogue’s Ark and read aloud on Saturday mornings. For 10 points, name this scripture that begins with Genesis.

tossups.p: On a fall holiday whose Hebrew name means “Rejoicing of” this text, people dance in seven circles around the synagogue while carrying it. On that holiday, readers finish its last passage and immediately begin again at its first words, “In the beginning.”
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Jewish scripture, the first five books of the Hebrew Bible, which is read aloud in sections each week.

tossups.p: According to the Letter of Aristeas [“uh-RISS-tee-us”], seventy-two Jewish scholars translated this text into Greek in Alexandria for King Ptolemy [“TOL-uh-mee”] II, beginning the translation known as the Septuagint. Another name for this text comes from the Greek word for “five.”
tossups.r: In the Tanakh, it comes before the Prophets and the Writings. For 10 points, name this scripture that runs from Genesis to Deuteronomy.

tossups.p: A rabbi in the Talmud counted 613 commandments in this text: 248 positive commands, matching the number of parts of the human body, and 365 prohibitions, one for each day of the solar year. Maimonides [“my-MON-ih-deez”] listed every one of them in his _Book of the Commandments_.
tossups.r: Jewish tradition holds that God gave this text to Moses at Mount Sinai. For 10 points, name this scripture made up of Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, and Deuteronomy.

tossups.p: In the Book of Nehemiah, the scribe Ezra stands on a wooden platform and reads this text aloud to the people of Jerusalem from early morning until midday, while Levites explain its meaning. The Sadducees held to this written law but rejected the oral traditions of the Pharisees.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Jewish scripture, which tradition says was given to Moses at Mount Sinai.

tossups.p: The Samaritans keep their own version of this text, written in an old form of the Hebrew alphabet, and they accept no other books as holy scripture. Muslims honor it as a holy book revealed to the prophet Musa.
tossups.r: Its first book is Genesis. For 10 points, name this scripture, the first part of the Hebrew Bible.

tossups.p: After a reading in the synagogue, one person lifts this open scroll high to show the congregation, and another rolls it closed and, in many synagogues, dresses it in a cloth cover and silver ornaments. It is kept in a cabinet called the Ark on the wall that faces Jerusalem.
tossups.r: Readers follow its text with a pointer called a yad, meaning “hand.” For 10 points, name this scroll of the first five books of the Hebrew Bible.

tossups.p: A famous passage of the Mishnah says that Moses received this text at Sinai and handed it down to Joshua, Joshua to the elders, the elders to the prophets, and the prophets to the Men of the Great Assembly.
tossups.r: Rabbis teach that an oral law explaining it was later written down in the Mishnah. For 10 points, name this written scripture of Judaism, whose five books begin with Genesis.

tossups.p: Julius Wellhausen [“VEL-how-zen”] popularized the theory that this text was woven together from four older sources, called J, E, D, and P. The source called D is named for its last book, which is mostly made up of Moses’s farewell speeches to the Israelites.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this collection of five books, beginning with Genesis, that is the holiest text of Judaism.

tossups.p: The books of this text have Hebrew names taken from words near their beginnings, such as Shemot [“sheh-MOHT”], meaning “names,” and Bamidbar [“bah-mid-BAR”], meaning “in the wilderness.” Its third book, Leviticus, is full of laws about priests, offerings, and holiness.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this scripture whose five books run from Genesis to Deuteronomy.

tossups.p: This text is divided into fifty-four weekly portions, and short sections of it are also read in synagogues on Monday and Thursday mornings. A bar mitzvah or bat mitzvah often chants a passage from it for the first time in front of the congregation.
tossups.r: Most synagogues read the whole thing once a year. For 10 points, name this Jewish scripture whose first book is Genesis.

tossups.p: Shavuot [“shah-voo-OHT”], which comes seven weeks after Passover, celebrates the day that Jewish tradition says God gave this text at Mount Sinai, and many people stay up all night on Shavuot to study it.
tossups.r: That text includes the Ten Commandments, which appear in both Exodus and Deuteronomy. For 10 points, name this scripture, the first five books of the Hebrew Bible.

tossups.p: Passages from this text are written on tiny parchment scrolls placed inside a mezuzah [“meh-ZOO-zuh”] on a doorpost and inside the small leather boxes called tefillin [“teh-FIL-in”]. One of those passages, the Shema [“shuh-MAH”], comes from its fifth book, Deuteronomy.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Jewish scripture, which tradition says Moses received on Mount Sinai.

tossups.p: As traditionally counted, the last of the 613 commandments in this text tells every Jew to write a copy of it, so many people help pay for a new scroll and take part in filling in its final letters. Worn-out scrolls of this text are not thrown away but are buried, often in a Jewish cemetery.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this scroll of the first five books of the Hebrew Bible, kept in a synagogue’s Ark.

trap.title: Torah, Tanakh, or Talmud?
trap.body: Several Jewish texts sound alike. The Torah is the five books from Genesis to Deuteronomy, written on the scrolls kept in synagogues. The Tanakh is the whole Hebrew Bible, of which the Torah is only the first part, so naming it earns just a prompt. The Talmud is a later collection of rabbinic discussion built on the Mishnah, and naming a single book, such as Genesis, is wrong too.
trap.fix: A scroll, a sofer, a yad, Simchat Torah, the 613 commandments, or “Genesis through Deuteronomy” mean the Torah (“Pentateuch” and “Five Books of Moses” also work). Rabbis debating, the Gemara, or “six orders” mean the Talmud or Mishnah. If the clues add the Prophets and the Writings, the answer is the Tanakh.
trap.line: Real answer line: Torah (or Pentateuch or Five Books of Moses; accept Chumash or Tawrat; prompt on Tanakh, Hebrew Bible, or Old Testament; do not accept “Talmud”)
